title: Vacuum-tube revival: nano vacuum-channel field-emission access switch
idea: Adapted from vacuum tubes and the thermos flask: replace the silicon access transistor with a gated nano vacuum channel (sharp Si or Mo emitter tip, 10-20 nm sealed vacuum gap, gate ring) that conducts by field emission only when the wordline raises the tip field. With the gate low, electrons must tunnel through the full vacuum barrier, so there is no junction, no GIDL and no subthreshold diffusion path.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3): off-current set by vacuum tunneling could be <1 aA, pushing retention from 64 ms toward minutes and cutting refresh energy >100x; risks are emitter wear, drive voltage and hermetic sealing at cell pitch.

title: Coal-mine canary cells that call for refresh only when needed
idea: Adapted from mining canaries and aviation condition-based maintenance: each subarray carries a few sentinel cells built with ~30% less storage capacitance and a longer gate-drain overlap, so they decay faster than the worst real cell. A tiny comparator polls them, and the bank is refreshed only when a sentinel crosses its threshold, not on a worst-case 32/64 ms timer.
why: Refresh is sized for the worst cell at the worst temperature; sentinels that track real temperature, voltage and aging let typical parts refresh 4-10x less often, cutting the 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth loss (fact 3).

title: Canal-lock access: series switches with an equalized middle chamber
idea: Adapted from canal locks, which equalize a chamber before opening a gate: put two access transistors in series and drive their middle node with a minimum-size follower whose gate is the storage node, so the inner transistor always sees ~0 V drain-source. Both gates open together for read/write; in hold, the storage-side device has almost no Vds to drive leakage.
why: Subthreshold leakage scales with (1 - exp(-Vds/kT/q)); holding Vds near 0 on the inner device cuts its leakage 10-100x and removes it from the retention tail (fact 3), at the cost of extra vertical transistors that 3D tiers could hide.

title: Solar PERC passivation: negative-charge AlOx liner around storage junctions
idea: Adapted from the PERC solar cell's field-effect passivation: line the buried-wordline trench and storage-node contact sidewalls with 2-5 nm ALD Al2O3, which carries ~1e12-1e13 cm^-2 fixed negative charge. The charge accumulates holes at the p-type surface, starving interface traps near the storage-node junction of the depletion they need to generate leakage current.
why: Solar makers cut surface recombination 10-100x this way; aimed at the access-device junction it targets the trap-dominated leakage tail (fact 3), plausibly doubling worst-cell retention with one extra ALD step and no EUV.

title: Power-MOSFET superjunction pillars inside the vertical access transistor
idea: Adapted from the superjunction in high-voltage power MOSFETs: build the vertical-channel access device with alternating thin p and n columns, charge-balanced so they fully deplete sideways. This flattens the electric-field peak at the drain/storage-node edge where band-to-band tunneling (GIDL) originates.
why: GIDL rises exponentially with peak field; a 30-40% lower peak could cut tail leakage 10-100x (fact 3) without a thicker oxide or longer channel, keeping the 4F2 vertical-channel footprint.

title: High-voltage cable stress-grading spacer that defuses the GIDL hotspot
idea: Adapted from stress-grading sleeves at HV cable terminations, which use high or field-dependent permittivity to spread equipotentials at the shield cut: form the gate-drain spacer of the buried-wordline device from a graded-k stack (high-k at the gate corner fading to low-k toward the storage node). The field at the overlap corner is spread over a longer distance instead of peaking.
why: The gate-edge corner is where GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling concentrate; grading the field there could cut the leakage tail about 10x (fact 3) and permit a deeper negative wordline for lower subthreshold leakage.

title: Image-sensor pinned-photodiode storage node with a transfer gate
idea: Adapted from the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: store the bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well capped by a p+ pinning layer, isolated from every Si/SiO2 interface, and move it to a floating diffusion through a transfer gate. A source follower reads it like a 4T pixel, so ~1-3k electrons suffice instead of ~30k.
why: Pinned photodiodes reach dark currents of a few electrons per second (~aA) at room temperature, ~10^4x below the 13 fA tail (fact 3); retention of seconds nearly removes refresh and the need for a 60-75:1 capacitor (fact 1), at 3-4 transistors per cell.

title: Image-sensor black-reference rows let the sense threshold track decay
idea: Adapted from the optical-black reference pixels image sensors use to subtract dark current: every row stores a few reference cells written to 1 and 0 at the same moment as the data. On read, a charge-sharing averager builds the sense reference from those cells' decayed levels instead of a fixed VDD/2.
why: A fixed reference loses margin as stored 1s sag; a self-decaying reference keeps the decision point centered, roughly doubling usable retention and allowing 2x longer refresh intervals at the same error rate (fact 3) for ~1% area.

title: Deep-space soft-decision LDPC reading of decayed DRAM charge
idea: Adapted from the soft-decision LDPC decoding used by deep-space probes and 5G: a dual-threshold sense amplifier produces a 2-bit confidence value per cell before latching, and an on-die LDPC decoder over 512-bit codewords uses that soft information. Cells that have decayed near threshold are corrected rather than refreshed pre-emptively.
why: Soft decoding tolerates raw bit-error rates near 1e-3 versus ~1e-15 for hard reads, letting the refresh interval grow 8-16x (fact 3) and cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss proportionally, for ~6% parity overhead.

title: Water-utility night pressure reduction: idle-mode rebias of array wells
idea: Adapted from utilities that lower mains pressure at night because leakage scales with pressure: when the DRAM enters self-refresh, it raises the array p-well bias toward 0 V (cutting the storage-junction field that drives trap-assisted leakage) and deepens the wordline-off voltage to hold subthreshold leakage, then restores active-mode biases on exit.
why: Active-mode biases are chosen for speed and row-hammer margin; idle mode can sit at the leakage minimum. Junction-field relief can cut tail leakage 2-5x, stretching self-refresh intervals proportionally (fact 3) at no area cost.

title: District-metered well taps measure each subarray's real leakage
idea: Adapted from water districts that find leaks by metering minimum night flow per zone: give each subarray its own isolated p-well with a metered tap. During idle, an on-die current integrator reads the well current (where junction and GIDL leakage ends up), sets that subarray's refresh rate from the measurement, and flags sudden jumps caused by VRT or aging.
why: Replaces a global worst-case assumption with measured per-subarray leakage, letting cool, healthy subarrays refresh 2-8x less (fact 3) and catching variable-retention-time cells that one-time profiling misses.

title: Cargo load-planning: per-row data masks keep weak cells discharged
idea: Adapted from ship load planning, which puts heavy cargo where the hull is strongest: using a factory map of weak-retention cells, every write picks one of four XOR scrambling masks (2 tag bits per row) so known weak cells hold the value their leakage pulls them toward. A cell already at its leakage endpoint cannot lose data.
why: Retention failures only hit cells holding the 'uphill' value; steering weak cells to safe values lets each row refresh at the rate of its strong cells, removing the tail from the refresh budget and cutting refresh 4x or more (fact 3) for ~0.4% tag overhead.

title: Regenerative-braking refresh: recycle bitline and wordline charge
idea: Adapted from regenerative braking: when one subarray finishes restoring a refreshed row, its high bitlines are connected through charge-sharing switches to the next subarray's bitlines before discharging, and wordlines are driven by an LC resonant (adiabatic) driver that returns wordline charge to a tank instead of ground.
why: Refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, fact 3) is mostly CV^2 from bitlines and the ~3 V wordline (fact 10); recovering half the bitline charge and most wordline charge could cut refresh energy 30-50%.

title: Scanning-tunneling-microscope gap switch: non-contact NEMS access device
idea: Adapted from the STM, whose current changes ~10x per angstrom of gap: a nano-cantilever tied to the storage node is pulled by the wordline from a 3 nm gap to ~0.8 nm from the bitline contact so electrons tunnel across in the on state. It never touches, so there is no contact wear, and at full gap tunneling current is ~1e-9 of on-current.
why: Removes the semiconductor junction from hold entirely, so off-leakage is set by vacuum tunneling (far below 1 aA) and retention could reach hours (fact 3); non-contact motion sidesteps the contact-wear endurance problem that stalled NEMS relays.

title: Photocopier-drum physics: optically gated photoconductor access switch
idea: Adapted from xerography, where a photoreceptor holds surface charge for minutes in the dark and discharges only where light hits: the access element is a wide-bandgap photoconductor (e.g., ZnO or a-SiC) switched by light pulses from an on-chip silicon-nitride waveguide 'wordline'. With no gate electrode there is no gate-induced drain leakage and no wordline CV^2.
why: Wide-bandgap photoconductor dark resistivity can exceed 1e14 ohm-cm, giving sub-aA hold leakage (fact 3) and removing the 3 V wordline swing (fact 10); the trade-offs are optical power budget and nanosecond photoconductor speed.

title: Qubit dynamical decoupling applied to variable-retention-time traps
idea: Adapted from the dynamical-decoupling pulse trains that protect qubits from noise: VRT cells toggle between low and high leakage when one defect near the junction changes charge state, so short periodic pulses on the plate or well bias (every few microseconds, ~10 ns wide) reset that defect into its low-leakage state before it can switch.
why: VRT forces vendors to guard-band refresh 2-4x above static profiles because weak cells cannot be found reliably; pinning the traps would let profiled multi-rate refresh (fact 3) run safely, cutting refresh 2-4x.

title: TCP congestion control applied to the refresh interval
idea: Adapted from TCP's additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease loop: each bank's refresh interval grows a step every epoch while patrol scrubs see zero ECC-corrected retention errors, and halves as soon as one appears, with a hard floor at JEDEC timing. Corrected errors play the role of packet loss.
why: Finds each part's real retention limit at its real temperature and age instead of the worst-case spec, typically 4-8x longer intervals in cool, lightly loaded systems (fact 3), with no new cell physics.

title: Solar advanced hydrogenation: light-assisted trap passivation of storage junctions
idea: Adapted from the PV industry's advanced hydrogenation, which uses intense illumination during a 200-400 C anneal to shift hydrogen into its mobile, reactive charge state: run it after the access-transistor module so hydrogen reaches and passivates the deep-level defects at the storage-node junction that create the leakage tail.
why: Tail cells are dominated by a few deep traps; passivating them could shrink the 13 fA tail 3-10x (fact 3) with low-cost tools that solar fabs already run at GW scale.

title: Check-valve cell: two opposing wide-bandgap diodes plus gain read
idea: Adapted from fluid check valves and the Tesla valve: the storage node is filled through one wide-bandgap diode from a 'fill' line and drained through a second, oppositely oriented diode to an 'empty' line. In hold, both lines park so both diodes are reverse-biased, and a read transistor gated by the storage node senses state without disturbing it.
why: Wide-bandgap heterojunction diodes (e.g., NiO/Ga2O3) can reverse-leak in the aA range, far below the 13 fA transistor tail (fact 3); thin-film diodes deposit above CMOS, which suits multi-tier 3D (fact 2).

title: Pharma cold chain: a refrigerated memory tier near minus 30 C
idea: Adapted from the pharmaceutical cold chain: capacity DIMMs sit in sealed, dry-nitrogen-purged sleds on a separate glycol loop chilled to about -30 C by a shared rack chiller, and the controller scales the refresh interval with measured die temperature.
why: Junction leakage roughly halves every 8-10 C, so going from 85 C to -30 C stretches retention 100-1000x and nearly removes refresh (fact 3); chiller energy is shared across a rack, and wires and transistors also speed up.

title: Electret-microphone charge sets the access-transistor threshold permanently
idea: Adapted from electret microphones, whose fluoropolymer holds implanted charge for decades: implant a stable sheet of fixed charge into a deep-trap dielectric layer beside the access channel so its threshold is raised permanently, letting the wordline rest at 0 V instead of a negative voltage when off.
why: The negative off-wordline adds gate-drain field that drives GIDL and needs always-on charge pumps; an electret-set threshold keeps subthreshold leakage low while cutting GIDL and removing the negative pump's standby power (facts 3, 10).

title: Pipeline cathodic protection: guard junctions intercept stray carriers
idea: Adapted from cathodic protection, where a sacrificial anode takes corrosion current instead of the pipe: run a shallow, reverse-biased n+ guard stripe between storage-node rows, tied to a collector rail, so minority electrons generated in the bulk or injected by hammered neighbor rows are collected before reaching a storage node.
why: Part of the leakage tail and much row-hammer charge loss is carrier diffusion through the substrate; a collector that grabs it could cut bulk-generated leakage several-fold (fact 3) and raise row-hammer thresholds (fact 9).

title: Class-D amplifier efficiency for wordline supplies: inductive switched VPP
idea: Adapted from the class-D audio amplifier's switch from linear to switched-mode conversion: replace the on-die Dickson charge pumps that make VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline voltage with an inductor-based buck-boost converter using package-embedded inductors, at 70-85% efficiency instead of ~25-35%.
why: Every refresh activation draws wordline charge from VPP; generating that charge 2-3x more efficiently cuts refresh and standby power substantially (facts 3, 10) without touching the cell.

title: Self-cleaning oven: wordline Joule heating anneals away the leakage tail
idea: Adapted from pyrolytic self-cleaning ovens and Macronix's self-healing NAND: during maintenance windows, drive a controlled current through selected buried wordlines to heat local cells to ~250-400 C for milliseconds, annealing traps and re-passivating interfaces that hot-carrier and hammer stress created over the module's life.
why: Repairable in place: rather than guard-banding refresh for end-of-life growth of the leakage tail (fact 3), the tail is periodically reset, extending service life and keeping refresh margins tight.

title: Self-healing concrete capsules: buried hydrogen reservoir re-passivates interfaces
idea: Adapted from self-healing concrete, which embeds capsules that release healing agent into new cracks: deposit a deuterium-rich SiNx reservoir film above the access-device level, capped by a barrier with a controlled leak rate, so D slowly re-supplies the Si/SiO2 interface and re-passivates dangling bonds as they form over a 10-year life.
why: Interface-trap generation drives leakage-tail growth with age (fact 3); a built-in healing supply keeps retention stable for longer and makes modules fit for second-life reuse instead of scrap.

title: Molybdenum roasting loop: tungsten-free, recoverable dual-work-function wordline
idea: Adapted from the molybdenum industry's purification route (roast to MoO3, which sublimes near 700 C and recondenses pure): make the buried wordline and contacts from Mo with a lower-work-function cap near the storage junction to cut GIDL, so the only refractory metal on the die is one that end-of-life roasting recovers cleanly.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) from the access device, lowers GIDL through the dual work function (fact 3), and gives scrap dies a simple metal-recovery route; Mo is mined in the U.S.

title: Wafer-reclaim Smart Cut: reusable donor wafer gives SOI access transistors
idea: Adapted from SOI layer transfer and the wafer-reclaim trade: cleave a thin single-crystal layer for the access transistors off a donor wafer by hydrogen implant, bond it onto oxide on the carrier, then repolish and reuse the donor 10+ times; the buried oxide removes the storage-junction-to-substrate leakage path.
why: Junction-to-substrate leakage is a main tail component (fact 3) and SOI removes it; donor reuse cuts consumption of CZ wafers grown in Spruce Pine quartz crucibles (resource chokepoint).

title: Solar junction-box bypass: power-gate and replace leaky mats in the field
idea: Adapted from the bypass diodes that route current around a shaded or cracked solar cell: each memory mat gets its own power gate and well switch plus a remap entry, so a mat whose leakage rises (seen in its refresh-error rate) is switched fully off and replaced by a spare mat in the same bank.
why: One leaky mat today forces the whole device to refresh faster or be scrapped; mat-level bypass repairs it in the field, removes its standby leakage, and keeps the rest of the die at a relaxed refresh rate (fact 3).

title: Circuit breakers, not fuses: resettable row repair held in MRAM
idea: Adapted from the move from one-time fuses to resettable breakers: replace laser-blown repair fuses with a small on-die MRAM remap table that can be rewritten without limit, so rows whose retention degrades or turns VRT are remapped, and later un-mapped, over the whole product life and through refurbishment.
why: Fuse and post-package repair are limited and mostly one-shot, so modules with drifting retention tails get scrapped; resettable repair keeps tail rows out of the refresh budget for life (fact 3) and makes refurbishment cheap.

title: SSD pSLC trick: aging regions downgrade to twin-cell differential mode
idea: Adapted from SSDs that run worn TLC blocks in pseudo-SLC mode: when telemetry shows a region's retention degrading, the controller reformats it so each bit uses two adjacent cells storing complementary charge, sensed differentially. The region loses half its capacity but gains ~4x retention and stays in service.
why: Graceful degradation instead of replacement: aging access devices (fact 3) no longer force faster refresh chip-wide or scrapping; capacity sheds in small steps and module life extends by years.

title: EV-battery second life: retention-graded DRAM cascade with refresh tags
idea: Adapted from the second-life market for retired EV batteries: the module SPD gains fields for a measured retention class and required refresh multiplier; retired server modules are re-profiled and resold into edge, PC or cache roles where 2x refresh or lower operating temperature is acceptable.
why: Raises usable supply without new wafers: modules with drifted leakage tails (fact 3) get a second service life instead of shredding, and the tags let controllers run them safely.

title: Battery direct recycling for dies: harvest and re-bond onto new base dies
idea: Adapted from direct cathode recycling, which restores battery material instead of smelting it: debond DRAM dies from retired modules, thin and retest them, then hybrid-bond them onto a new logic base die that holds a per-row retention map and issues row-specific refresh, so dies with drifted leakage run again behind a smarter refresh engine.
why: Reuses the most capital-heavy part, the EUV-patterned array (fact 4), and compensates aged access devices (fact 3) with new logic; each reused die avoids new fab capacity.

title: Aviation line-replaceable units: swappable refresh-and-periphery die
idea: Adapted from aircraft line-replaceable units, built to be swapped on the flight line: split each DRAM into an array die (cells, access devices, sense amps) and a separately mounted periphery die carrying refresh scheduling, temperature sensing, ECC and retention maps, joined by a reworkable fine-pitch interposer, so the refresh brain is upgraded or replaced without discarding the array.
why: Arrays outlive their refresh logic; a replaceable refresh engine lets old arrays gain new retention-aware algorithms (fact 3) and moves part of the 49% periphery area (fact 7) onto a cheaper node.

title: Set-top-box firmware updates: on-die microcoded refresh sequencer
idea: Adapted from over-the-air firmware updates: replace the hard-wired refresh counter with a tiny on-die microcontroller running signed microcode (refresh ordering, multi-rate bins, temperature curves, row-hammer mitigations), updatable by the host through a mode-register channel for the module's whole life.
why: Refresh and row-hammer policy can be repaired after deployment as new leakage behavior or attacks appear (facts 3, 9), instead of replacing hardware, keeping modules in service longer.

title: Vehicle history report: retention passport and stress odometer per die
idea: Adapted from vehicle history reports and odometers: each die keeps a write-protected record of its factory retention bins and weak-cell map, plus counters for hot hours, activations and refresh-error events, readable by any refurbisher through a standard command.
why: Retention testing a used module takes hours at temperature, which kills reuse economics; a trusted passport lets refurbishers re-grade modules in seconds and set safe second-life refresh rates (fact 3).

title: Farm-equipment right-to-repair: open retention and repair command standard
idea: Adapted from the right-to-repair rules won for farm equipment: a JEDEC requirement backed by federal procurement rules that vendors publish the commands to read retention maps, trigger post-package repair and set refresh multipliers, so independent shops can repair and re-grade modules.
why: Third parties cannot repair retention-degraded modules today, so they are scrapped; open repair interfaces expand usable supply and seed U.S. refurbishment work without new fabs (fact 3, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Jet-engine power-by-the-hour: vendors sell retained gigabyte-hours
idea: Adapted from Rolls-Royce's power-by-the-hour model: DRAM vendors lease modules and are paid per GB-hour of error-free service, keep ownership, watch retention telemetry remotely, and swap, anneal or re-grade modules before leakage tails cause errors.
why: Gives the maker a profit motive to design repairable, long-lived access devices and to refurbish (fact 3), turning installed DRAM into a reused fleet asset rather than a disposable part.

title: Plumbing unions for 3D stacks: reworkable low-temperature microbump joints
idea: Adapted from plumbing unions that let one pipe section come out without cutting the rest: bond HBM-style stacks with low-melting In or Sn-Bi microbumps at defined 'union' levels, so a die whose retention fails burn-in or ages in the field can be removed near 150 C and replaced without scrapping the stack.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% (fact 6), often from one weak die; reworkable unions recover the other dies and let leaky dies (fact 3) be swapped instead of guard-banding refresh for the whole stack.

title: Film-capacitor self-clearing: a pulse burns out each leakage path
idea: Adapted from self-clearing metallized film capacitors, whose thin electrode vaporizes around a breakdown spot to isolate it: make the storage-node top electrode an ultrathin film and apply a controlled clearing pulse to cells that test leaky, so the electrode opens or oxidizes locally at the leakage path while the rest keeps most of the capacitance.
why: Turns dielectric leakage defects in the tail (facts 1, 3) into repairable events at test or in the field rather than row replacement or faster refresh; a cleared cell keeps working with slightly lower capacitance.

title: LCD panel laser repair: spot-anneal the retention-tail cells
idea: Adapted from the laser repair stations that fix defective TFT pixels in LCD fabs: after retention test, or at a refurbisher, a nanosecond laser heats ~1 um spots containing weak cells through a thinned backside in forming gas, annealing the traps that cause their leakage.
why: Repairs the leakage tail (fact 3) of finished dies without spending spare rows; LCD fabs run such tools at high throughput, and repair can be repeated at end of first life before resale.

title: Solar PID-recovery box: nightly reverse-bias de-trapping of access devices
idea: Adapted from the PID-recovery boxes that undo potential-induced degradation in solar parks with a night-time counter-voltage: during idle windows the controller applies reverse gate and well bias to blocks of rows for seconds, emptying charge trapped in access-transistor gate dielectrics and spacers by wordline and hammer stress.
why: Trapped charge raises leakage and causes drift over life (fact 3); routine recovery undoes it, keeping retention near day-one values and delaying replacement.

title: LED constant-lumen drivers: aging-compensated negative wordline trim per mat
idea: Adapted from LED drivers that raise current as LEDs age to hold light output constant: each mat carries a replica access transistor whose leakage is measured monthly, and a small trim DAC deepens that mat's off-wordline voltage step by step to hold replica leakage at its day-one value, logging the trim history for refurbishers.
why: Compensates access-device aging in place (fact 3), so factory refresh settings stay valid over a 10-year life and second-life modules need no slower refresh.

title: Railway wheel re-profiling: per-cell charge injection retunes leaky transistors
idea: Adapted from underfloor wheel lathes that re-profile train wheels without removing them: for each cell flagged as leaky, a high-field write sequence injects charge into that access transistor's drain-side spacer, relieving its gate-edge field or raising its local threshold until leakage meets spec; it can be repeated in the field.
why: Repairs individual tail cells (fact 3) without spare rows or global bias changes, so the tail is trimmed as it appears and the whole array refreshes at the strong-cell rate.

title: Piano tuning: periodic field re-trim of sense-amplifier offsets
idea: Adapted from routine piano tuning: each sense amplifier has a small offset-trim capacitor bank whose setting is stored in non-volatile cells, and a maintenance routine re-measures offsets with known test levels every few months and re-tunes them as transistors drift.
why: Sense-amp offset consumes a large share of the retention signal margin; keeping it trimmed for life allows perhaps 30-50% more decay, so refresh intervals stay long as parts age (fact 3), and refurbishers re-tune instead of scrapping.

title: Bottle-deposit systems: refundable deposit funds module retention re-profiling
idea: Adapted from container-deposit schemes: add a refundable deposit (~$2-5) to each memory module, redeemable at certified refurbishers that re-profile retention, remap weak rows and re-grade modules into refresh classes; unredeemed deposits fund the re-test equipment.
why: Most retired DRAM is shredded before anyone checks whether its access devices still retain data (fact 3); a deposit captures modules for re-grading and adds usable supply without new fabs.

title: Airline heavy-check rotation: drain, heal and return pooled memory live
idea: Adapted from airlines rotating aircraft through heavy checks while the fleet keeps flying: in a CXL memory pool, the fabric manager live-migrates data off a module flagged by retention telemetry, runs a service cycle on it (full retention re-profile, bias recovery, row repair), then returns it, with ~5% spare capacity covering modules in service.
why: Makes in-field retention repair routine with zero downtime (fact 3), so pools can run aggressive relaxed refresh knowing degraded modules are healed before they fail, and modules stay in service longer.
